🌀 Thrashing & the Working Set

THE FAILURE MODE
Thrashing: collective memory needs exceed physical RAM → every process faults, evicting each other's pages endlessly. Signature: CPU utilization PLUMMETS while disk I/O SPIKES — the system pages instead of working. Counter-intuitively worst when running the MOST processes.
THE WORKING-SET MODEL
Working set = the pages a process touched in the last τ time units (it shifts as program phases change). Resident set = pages actually in RAM. The strategy: only schedule a process if its working set FITS; if the total exceeds memory, SUSPEND some processes until the rest can run fault-free. Simpler reactive alternative — Page Fault Frequency (PFF): fault rate too high → give frames; too low → take frames. It all works because of locality of reference: programs access clustered addresses over short windows.
THE RESPONSE PLAYBOOK + MODERN REALITY
Detect: paging activity high + CPU low. Respond: reduce the degree of multiprogramming, or add memory. Modern systems: big servers rarely thrash; mobile/cloud prefer OOM kill and explicit memory limits over degraded swapping. Swap is NOT "extra RAM" — it's orders of magnitude slower.
⚠️ FOR PROGRAMMERS
Memory pressure shows up as terrible LATENCY long before anything is killed. Watch page-fault rate, swap activity, and resident set size — a box with a calm CPU graph can be unusably slow from paging. Keep headroom.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
CPU utilization drops sharply while disk activity spikes. The likely diagnosis is:
  1. Thrashing — reduce multiprogramming or add memory
  2. A faster disk
  3. Deadlock
  4. TLB overflow
Show answer + steps
A. The classic signature: the system spends its time swapping pages, not computing. Suspend processes or add RAM.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

If processes collectively need more pages than physical memory holds, the system spends more time paging than computing — thrashing. The working-set model and related ideas detect and prevent it. Understanding thrashing is essential for capacity planning and diagnosing 'why is the system suddenly so slow?'

Core concepts

1. What thrashing looks like. CPU utilization plummets, disk I/O spikes, response times collapse. Processes fault on pages, evict another process's pages, that process faults — endless replacement with no useful work. User perception: 'system is stuck.' Real failure mode.

2. The cause: insufficient frames per process. If each process has too few resident frames to hold its currently-needed pages, every memory access nearly faults. Counter-intuitive but real: the system is most memory-starved when running the most processes — opposite of intent.

3. The working set. The set of pages a process has accessed in the last τ time units. If the working set fits in physical memory, faults are rare. If not, thrashing. The working set changes over time as program phases change (initialization → steady state → cleanup).

4. Working set strategy. Track each process's working set; only schedule it to run if its working set fits. If total working sets exceed memory, suspend some processes (move out of ready queue) until the rest can run without thrashing. Crude but effective.

5. Page fault frequency (PFF) heuristic. Watch each process's fault rate. Above a high threshold: give it more frames. Below a low threshold: take frames away. Reactive, simpler than tracking working sets explicitly.

6. Modern systems and swap. Servers with abundant RAM rarely thrash. Mobile and laptops have small swap; aggressive memory pressure triggers OOM kill rather than degraded paging. Cloud workloads tune memory limits explicitly to avoid both swap and OOM.

7. The lesson for programmers. Memory pressure surfaces as terrible latency long before processes get killed. Monitor fault rate, swap activity, resident set size. A box that looks fine on CPU graphs can be unusably slow because of paging. Always keep memory headroom.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Overcommitting memory to maximize utilization — slope from 'tight' to 'thrashing' is sudden.
  • Assuming swap is 'extra memory' — it's orders of magnitude slower than RAM.
  • Ignoring page fault rate as a metric — most direct signal of memory pressure.
  • Tuning processes individually without considering aggregate working set — interaction effects are real.

Quick recap

Thrashing happens when collective working sets exceed physical memory; the system pages itself to a halt. Working-set model tracks pages used recently and admits only processes whose working sets fit. PFF is a simpler reactive heuristic. Modern cloud systems avoid swap and use memory limits + OOM kill. Page fault rate is the signal to watch.

Glossary

Thrashing
Pathological state where the system spends most time paging instead of computing.
Working set
Set of pages a process has accessed in a recent time window.
Resident set
Pages of a process actually in physical memory at a given moment.
Page fault frequency (PFF)
Rate of faults; heuristic for memory pressure.
Swap
Disk-backed extension of virtual memory; orders of magnitude slower than RAM.

Thrashing: detection = paging activity high while CPU utilization drops — the system spends its time swapping, not working. Response strategy: reduce the degree of multiprogramming (or add memory), and use a working-set strategy that adjusts each process’s frames to what it actually touches. All of it works because of locality of reference — programs access clustered addresses over short windows.

📄 Files, Directories & Permissions

WHAT A FILE IS (OS-SIDE)
A named, persistent collection of bytes + metadata the OS keeps for it: size, type, owner, permissions, timestamps, location. Your program sees bytes; the OS does the bookkeeping. Every operation (create/open/read/write/seek/close/delete/rename/truncate) maps to a system call; open returns a file descriptor (Unix) or handle (Windows) used by everything after.
FILE ATTRIBUTES & DIRECTORY STRUCTURE
AttributeMeaning
Name · IdentifierHuman name · inode number (Unix)
Typeregular · directory · symlink · device
Location · SizeWhere on disk · byte count
Protection · TimestampsPermissions · created/modified/accessed
Directory structures evolved: single-level → two-level (per-user) → hierarchical tree (modern). Each directory maps names → inodes; paths traverse the tree (/home/user/file.txt).
ACCESS MODES + UNIX PERMISSION MODEL
Sequential = read/write in order from the current position (like tape). Direct/random = seek to any position (standard for disk files). Unix permissions = nine bits: read/write/execute × owner/group/other, shown by ls -l as rwxr-xr--. ACLs extend this for finer control; Windows uses a richer ACL model.
⚠️ FOUR TRAPS
Hard link (another name for the SAME inode) ≠ symlink (a path pointing to a path). Unix ctime is metadata-change time, NOT creation. Build paths with OS-aware utilities, not string concatenation. And execute on a directory means "can traverse into it," not "run it."

  2. The file's full contents
  3. The inode's raw bytes
  4. A permission string
Show answer + steps

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Files are the longest-lived, most user-visible OS abstraction. Every program reads or writes them. Every backup, every deployment, every security policy is built on file semantics — names, permissions, types, timestamps. Understanding the interface is foundational.

Core concepts

1. What a file is, OS-side. A named, persistent collection of bytes. The OS associates metadata: size, type, owner, permissions, timestamps, location. Programs see the bytes; the OS bookkeeping happens behind the scenes.

2. File operations. create, open, read, write, seek, close, delete, rename, truncate. Each maps to a system call. open returns a file descriptor (Unix) or handle (Windows) used by subsequent operations. Most file APIs are skin over these primitives.

3. File attributes. Name. Identifier (inode number on Unix). Type (regular, directory, symlink, device). Location (where on disk). Size. Protection (permissions). Timestamps (created, modified, accessed). Each accessible via stat() or equivalent.

4. Directory structures. Single-level (early systems): one big directory. Two-level: per-user directories. Hierarchical (modern): tree of directories. Each directory maps names to inodes (or equivalent). Paths traverse the tree: /home/user/file.txt.

5. Sequential vs direct (random) access. Sequential: read or write data in order from current position. Like a tape. Direct: jump to any position via seek. Standard for files on disk. Sequential is sometimes more efficient (no seek overhead); direct is more flexible.

6. File types and extensions. OS-level types: regular file, directory, symlink, FIFO, socket, device. Convention-level types: indicated by extension (.txt, .pdf, .jpg). Some OSes enforce types; Unix mostly doesn't (extensions are convention).

7. Permissions (Unix model). Three permission bits — read, write, execute — for three classes — owner, group, other. ls -l shows them as rwxr-xr--. ACLs extend this with finer control. Windows uses richer ACL-based model. The Unix nine-bit model is simple and ubiquitous.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS

  • Treating timestamps as exact creation times — Unix ctime is metadata change time, not creation. Modern systems track creation separately.
  • Building paths by string concatenation across platforms — '/' vs '' bites; use OS-aware path utilities.
  • Forgetting that 'execute' on a directory means 'can traverse into it' — different from execute on a file.

Quick recap

A file is named, persistent bytes plus metadata. Operations: create, open, read, write, seek, close, delete. Directory structures organize names hierarchically. Sequential vs direct access. File types span OS-level (regular, directory, symlink) and convention-level (extensions). Unix permissions: nine bits across owner, group, other. Foundation for everything else file-related.

Glossary

File
Named, persistent collection of bytes plus OS metadata.
Directory
Special file mapping names to file IDs (inodes).
File descriptor
Per-process integer handle returned by open.
Permissions
Access controls per file: read, write, execute for owner/group/other.
Path
String identifying a file's location in the directory hierarchy.

🗄️ File System Implementation

THE THREE LAYERS
Top: FS API (open/read/write) · Middle: FS implementation (inodes, blocks, allocation) · Bottom: block device driver. Each layer abstracts the one below — debugging often means reasoning downward through them.
INODES + ALLOCATION METHODS
An inode holds a file's metadata + pointers to its data blocks; a directory entry maps a name → inode number. Many names can point to one inode (hard links). Inodes are pre-allocated — running out means "disk full" even with free bytes.
AllocationTrade-off
ContiguousFast read, hard to grow
LinkedEasy growth, slow random access
IndexedThe winner — index block lists data blocks (ext4, NTFS, APFS)
REAL FILE SYSTEMS + FREE SPACE
FAT (FAT32/exFAT): a table at the volume start, each entry points to the next block. Universal (USB, SD) but no permissions, size limits. NTFS: journaling, ACLs, hard links, encryption (Windows default). ext4: journaling, extents, online defrag (Linux default). Free space tracked by bitmap (one bit per block — compact, parallelizable; what modern FS use) or free list. The buffer/page cache keeps recently-used disk blocks in RAM — the FS's speed trick, powered by locality.
⚠️ FOUR TRAPS
Millions of tiny files can exhaust inodes despite free space. write() lands in the page cache, not disk — fsync forces the flush. Never compare FS performance without naming the workload. Don't pick FAT when you need permissions or large files.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Which allocation method do modern file systems favor for growth-friendly storage?
  1. Indexed allocation
  2. Contiguous allocation
  3. Linked allocation
  4. No allocation
Show answer + steps
A. Indexed allocation (an index block listing data blocks) balances random-access speed with easy growth — used by ext4, NTFS, APFS.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Beneath the familiar file-system API sits a careful design — inodes, blocks, free lists, journals. Each layer trades performance for reliability or vice versa. Knowing how a file system actually stores data explains its strengths, limits, and why some operations are surprisingly slow.

Core concepts

1. Layered structure. Top: file system API (open, read, write). Middle: file system implementation (inodes, blocks, allocation). Bottom: block device driver. Each layer abstracts the layer below; debugging often requires reasoning down through them.

2. Inodes — the heart of Unix-style FS. An inode holds a file's metadata and pointers to its data blocks. A directory entry maps a name to an inode number. Same file can have many directory entries (hard links) all pointing to one inode. Inodes are pre-allocated; running out means 'disk full' even with bytes free.

3. Allocation methods. Contiguous: file in one extent. Fast read, hard to grow. Linked: blocks form a chain. Easy growth, slow random access. Indexed: an index block lists data blocks. The hybrid winner — used by ext4, NTFS, APFS. Each method handles fragmentation differently.

4. FAT — File Allocation Table. Used by FAT32, exFAT. A table at the start of the volume; each entry points to the next block of the file. Simple and ubiquitous (USB drives, SD cards). Limitations: no permissions, max file size, fragmentation handling. Universal compatibility keeps it alive.

5. NTFS — Windows file system. Modern replacement for FAT. Journaling, ACLs, hard links, alternate data streams, encryption. Widely used; understood well. Default on Windows.

6. ext4 — Linux's standard. Successor to ext2/ext3. Journaling, extents (better than block lists for large files), online defragmentation. Solid, well-understood, default on most Linux distributions. Newer alternatives (Btrfs, ZFS, XFS) compete in some niches.

7. Free space management. Track which blocks are free. Bitmap: one bit per block, scanned for free ones. Free list: linked list of free blocks. Bitmaps are compact and parallelizable; free lists need no scan but lose locality. Modern FS use bitmaps.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Running out of inodes despite free space — happens with millions of tiny files.
  • Treating write() as 'on disk now' — it's in the page cache; fsync forces flush.
  • Comparing FS performance without specifying workload — sequential, random, small, large all matter differently.
  • Choosing FAT for a system needing permissions or large files — FAT lacks both.

Quick recap

File systems use inodes for metadata, blocks for data, indexed allocation for growth-friendly storage. Free-block bitmaps track availability. Page cache makes reads fast. FAT is universal but limited; NTFS, ext4, APFS are full-featured. Modern designs (ZFS, Btrfs) add CoW and snapshots. Layering enables generic APIs over diverse implementations.

Glossary

Inode
Per-file structure holding metadata and pointers to data blocks.
Block
Fixed-size unit of disk allocation (typically 4 KB).
Indexed allocation
Block-allocation strategy using an index block listing data blocks.
FAT
File Allocation Table; simple FS used on USB drives, SD cards.
NTFS / ext4
Modern file systems with journaling and extended permissions.

The buffer cache: the OS caches file-system reads and writes in main memory — recently used disk blocks are served from RAM, and writes can be batched. It is the file system’s speed trick, powered by locality.

💽 Disk Scheduling

THE HDD SEEK PROBLEM
Moving the head between tracks (a seek) costs milliseconds — the slow part. Sequential reads (no head movement) are ~100× faster than random. So the order of requests determines total seek time, and that's what these algorithms optimize.
THE FIVE ALGORITHMS
AlgorithmRuleWatch out
FCFSServe in arrival orderSimple; often wasteful under load
SSTFClosest request to head nextBig seek savings but starvation — needs aging
SCANElevator: sweep one way serving all, then reverseBounded, fair
C-SCANSweep ONE direction only, jump back at endMore uniform waits — fairer to outer tracks
LOOK / C-LOOKLike SCAN/C-SCAN but only as far as outstanding requestsThe real-world default
SSDs CHANGE EVERYTHING
SSDs have uniform read times — no head to move — so seek-minimizing algorithms make no sense on flash. Linux uses noop or mq-deadline for SSDs; modern systems detect the device type and adjust automatically.
⚠️ FOUR TRAPS
SCAN/C-SCAN on an SSD wastes effort on a non-problem. SSTF without aging starves far-out requests. Interactive (latency) vs bulk (throughput) requests want different policies. And real time = seek + rotational latency, not seek alone.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Which algorithm risks starving requests far from the current head position?
  1. SSTF
  2. SCAN
  3. C-SCAN
  4. FCFS
Show answer + steps
A. SSTF always picks the closest request, so a steady stream of nearby requests can starve distant ones — mitigate with aging.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

On spinning disks, the order of I/O requests drastically affects throughput. The disk scheduling algorithms — FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK — minimize seek time. On SSDs the calculus changes, but understanding the classical algorithms remains foundational and may appear on exams.

Core concepts

1. The HDD seek problem. Moving the head between tracks (seek) is the slow part — milliseconds per move. Sequential reads, where the head doesn't move, are 100x faster than random ones. The order of requests determines total seek time.

2. FCFS — First-Come, First-Served. Serve in arrival order. Simple. Often suboptimal: if requests come in a bad order, total seek distance is large. Good for low-load systems where requests are rare; otherwise wasteful.

3. SSTF — Shortest Seek Time First. Serve the request closest to the current head position. Reduces total seek time substantially. Risk: starvation — far-out requests may wait while nearby requests keep arriving. Common but needs aging or other safeguards.

4. SCAN — the elevator algorithm. Head moves in one direction, serving all requests in its path. At the end, reverses. Like an elevator. Bounded wait time; fair. Simple to implement. Used as baseline in Unix-like systems for years.

5. C-SCAN — Circular SCAN. Head moves one direction only, jumping back to the start at the end (no service on the return). More uniform wait times — fairness for outermost tracks. Often preferred over SCAN when consistency matters.

6. LOOK and C-LOOK — refined SCAN. Like SCAN/C-SCAN but only sweep as far as the outstanding requests reach, not all the way to the end of the disk. More efficient. The default in many real implementations.

7. Disk scheduling on SSDs. SSDs have uniform read times; seek-minimizing algorithms don't apply. Linux's 'noop' or 'mq-deadline' schedulers are typically used for SSDs. Old SCAN-family algorithms make no sense on flash. Modern systems detect the device type and adjust.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Using SCAN/C-SCAN on SSDs — wastes effort on a non-problem.
  • SSTF without aging — far-out requests may starve.
  • Assuming all requests are equal — interactive (latency-sensitive) and bulk (throughput-sensitive) requests benefit from different policies.
  • Calculating total seek distance without considering rotation — seek + rotational latency together determine real time.

Quick recap

FCFS: simple, often inefficient. SSTF: closest first; risks starvation. SCAN: elevator-style sweep, both directions. C-SCAN: one direction only, fairer wait times. LOOK and C-LOOK: refined to only sweep outstanding range. SSDs make these algorithms obsolete; modern Linux uses noop or mq-deadline. Calculate seek time as a standard exam exercise.

Glossary

Seek time
Time for HDD head to move to a target track.
FCFS (First-Come, First-Served)
Serve disk requests in arrival order.
SSTF
Shortest Seek Time First; serve the closest request next.
SCAN / elevator
Sweep in one direction, then reverse; serves all requests on the way.
C-SCAN
Circular SCAN; sweep one direction only, jumping back at the end.

🔌 The I/O Subsystem

POLLING vs INTERRUPTS vs DMA (pick by device speed)
MethodHowBest for
PollingCPU repeatedly checks "ready?"Wasteful — only very fast/simple cases
InterruptsDevice signals CPU when ready; CPU works meanwhileMedium-speed devices
DMADevice moves data to/from RAM itself; CPU interrupted on completionHigh-throughput devices
Without DMA, every byte would pass through the CPU; with it, the CPU is free for real work.
THE SUPPORTING CAST
Kernel I/O subsystem is layered: drivers (bottom) → block/network layers → file system & sockets (top), providing queueing, scheduling, error handling, caching. Buffering smooths producer/consumer rate mismatches (single, double, circular buffers). Caching keeps recent data in faster memory — the Unix page cache is one of the most influential OS designs ever. Spooling queues requests for ordered/parallel service — print spooling is the classic example, and it lives on in message queues and async pipelines.
⚠️ FOUR TRAPS
Polling a slow device wastes CPU when interrupts would yield — yet at very high IOPS (NVMe), polling can beat interrupt overhead. Skipping DMA means byte-copying can exceed wire bandwidth. And synchronous I/O in high-throughput servers leaves the CPU idle — async multiplies throughput.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Which mechanism lets a device move data to/from RAM without the CPU copying each byte?
  1. DMA
  2. Polling
  3. Spooling
  4. Buffering
Show answer + steps
A. Direct Memory Access — the CPU sets up the transfer, the device does the bulk move, and the CPU is interrupted only on completion.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

I/O — disk, network, peripherals — connects the CPU to the rest of the world. The I/O subsystem's design (polling, interrupts, DMA, buffering) determines whether the CPU spends most of its time computing or waiting. Modern systems lean heavily on async I/O and DMA.

Core concepts

1. Polling vs interrupts vs DMA. Polling: CPU repeatedly checks if device is ready. Wasteful for slow devices. Interrupts: device signals CPU when ready; CPU does other work meanwhile. Standard for medium-speed devices. DMA: device transfers data directly to/from memory without CPU; CPU is interrupted on completion. Standard for high-throughput devices.

2. The interrupt mechanism. Device asserts an interrupt line. CPU finishes current instruction, saves state, jumps to interrupt handler. Handler reads device status, copies data, dismisses interrupt. CPU resumes. Modern systems handle hundreds of interrupts per second.

3. DMA — Direct Memory Access. Devices transfer data to and from RAM without CPU intervention. CPU sets up the transfer, device does the bulk move, CPU is interrupted on completion. Without DMA, every byte would pass through the CPU. With it, the CPU is free to do real work.

4. The kernel I/O subsystem. Layered: device drivers (per-device code) at the bottom; subsystem-specific layers (block layer, network stack); top-level interfaces (file system, sockets). Common services: queueing, scheduling, error handling, caching.

5. Buffering. Smooths out producer/consumer rate mismatches. CPU writes fast to a buffer; device drains slowly from it. Common patterns: single buffer, double buffering (one fills while the other empties), circular buffers. Buffering is everywhere in I/O paths.

6. Caching. Recently-read data kept in faster memory. Page cache for files, network cache for repeat requests, DNS cache for repeat lookups. Often the difference between fast and slow operation. The Unix page cache is one of the most influential designs in OS history.

7. Spooling. Older idea: queue I/O requests so they can be served in parallel or reordered for efficiency. Print spooling is the canonical example — print requests queued so users don't wait for the printer. Persists in batch processing, message queues, async pipelines.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Polling for fast devices — wastes CPU when interrupts would yield.
  • Polling slow devices when high IOPS — interrupt overhead exceeds gain; modern NVMe sometimes prefers polling.
  • Doing I/O without DMA — copying into and out of kernel buffers can exceed wire bandwidth.
  • Building synchronous I/O paths in high-throughput servers — CPU sits idle; async multiplies throughput.

Quick recap

I/O performance comes from drivers, DMA, buffering, and concurrency. Polling vs interrupts vs DMA pick coordination strategy by device speed. Buffering smooths rate mismatches; caching speeds repeat access; spooling queues for efficiency. The blocking → non-blocking → async progression scales servers to handle thousands of connections. Know the kernel I/O subsystem layers.

Glossary

DMA (Direct Memory Access)
Devices read/write RAM without CPU mediation.
Polling vs interrupts
Two ways the CPU learns the device is ready: actively checking vs receiving signals.
Buffering
Smoothing rate mismatches between producer and consumer via memory buffers.
Page cache
In-memory cache of file blocks; speeds repeat reads.
Spooling
Queuing I/O requests for ordered or parallel processing.

🛡️ Protection & Access Control

THE PROTECTION QUESTION
Who (subject) can do what (operation) to which object? Subject = user/process · Operation = read/write/execute/delete · Object = file/socket/process/device. Every access-control model answers this triple. The guiding rule: least privilege — each component gets only the permissions it actually needs, so a bug's blast radius stays small.
HOW ACCESS IS STORED
The access matrix (subjects × objects, cells = allowed operations) is the concept — too huge/sparse to store directly, so real systems use one of its slices:
StructureOrganized byGood at
ACLPer-object list of (subject, ops)"Who can read this file?" (NTFS, POSIX ACLs)
Capability listPer-subject tokens the subject holdsDelegation (file descriptors, OAuth tokens, seL4)
THE THREE MODELS (+ how they're realized)
ModelWho decidesExamples
DACOwners set accessUnix file permissions — flexible, error-prone
MACSystem-wide policy via labels (Top Secret…) overrides usersSELinux, AppArmor
RBACPermissions → roles, users → rolesDatabases, cloud IAM, enterprise apps
Mechanisms that enforce it: sudo/setuid (controlled, audited privilege escalation), sandboxing (limits what a process can touch regardless of bugs), and containers (isolated views of FS/network/processes — lighter than VMs).
⚠️ FOUR TRAPS
Running services as root "because easier" — compromise = total access. Unix permissions alone aren't enough for shared-user systems (need ACLs/RBAC). Leaving SELinux in permissive mode "to make it work" disables protection. Permanent capabilities are hard to revoke — grant temporarily.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Unix file permissions are an example of which model?
  1. DAC — owners decide access
  2. MAC — system policy decides
  3. RBAC — roles decide
  4. None of these
Show answer + steps
A. Discretionary Access Control: the file's owner sets who can read/write/execute — flexible but easy to misconfigure.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Multiuser systems must isolate users from each other and from the kernel. Protection is the mechanism. Knowing the models — DAC, MAC, RBAC, capabilities — and their concrete realizations (Unix permissions, ACLs, RBAC) is foundational to system security.

Core concepts

1. The protection question. Who can do what to which object? Subject (user, process). Operation (read, write, execute, delete). Object (file, socket, process, device). Every access control model answers this triple in some way.

2. Principle of least privilege. Every process should have only the permissions it actually needs. setuid binaries, dropped privileges after startup, separate service accounts. Older than every concrete mechanism. Violations are how exploitable bugs become catastrophic breaches.

3. The access matrix. Conceptual model: rows are subjects, columns are objects, cells say what operations subject can perform on object. Useful for reasoning; not directly stored (would be huge and sparse). Real systems use access control lists (per-object) or capability lists (per-subject) instead.

4. Access control lists (ACLs). Per-object: list of (subject, operations) pairs. NTFS, modern Linux (POSIX ACLs). Easy to ask 'who can read this file.' Less convenient to ask 'what can this user access.' Standard in modern OSes.

5. Capability lists. Per-subject: list of (object, operations) tokens the subject holds. Used in capability OSes (KeyKOS, seL4) and modern systems like file descriptors (a kind of capability) and OAuth tokens. Cleaner for delegation; less common as primary OS mechanism.

6. Discretionary vs Mandatory Access Control. DAC: owners decide who can access their resources. Unix file permissions are DAC. Flexible but error-prone. MAC: system-wide policy overrides individual users. Subjects and objects have labels (Top Secret, Secret); enforcement is automatic. SELinux, AppArmor.

7. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). Permissions assigned to roles; users assigned to roles. Easier admin than per-user permissions. Adopted everywhere — databases, cloud platforms (IAM), enterprise apps. Composes with DAC/MAC.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Running services as root because 'easier' — when compromised, root means total system access.
  • Treating Unix permissions as enough for shared-user systems — ACLs or RBAC may be needed.
  • Misconfiguring SELinux into permissive mode and forgetting to fix it — common 'works again' fix that disables protection.
  • Granting capabilities permanently when they should be temporary — once granted, hard to revoke.

Quick recap

DAC: owners control. MAC: system policy enforces labels. RBAC: roles bundle permissions. Capabilities: unforgeable tokens grant specific rights. Least privilege limits any one component's blast radius. Real systems combine these; defense in depth is the goal.

Glossary

DAC
Discretionary Access Control — owners set permissions.
MAC
Mandatory Access Control — system-wide policy overrides users.
RBAC
Role-Based Access Control — permissions via roles.
ACL (Access Control List)
Per-object list of who can do what.
Least privilege
Principle: each component has only the permissions it actually needs.

Security mechanisms: running a command as another user (sudo/setuid) is controlled privilege escalation — powerful and audited. Sandboxing restricts what a process can see and touch regardless of its bugs. Containers (Docker) package apps with isolated views of the filesystem, network, and processes — lighter than VMs, stronger than nothing.

📊 FIGURE — the ids a Unix process carries
🎯 EXAM TIP
GID is the Group Identifier and UID the User Identifier. Permission checks compare the process's effective ids against the file's owner and group — which is why setuid programs are security-sensitive: they deliberately run with the file owner's id instead of the caller's.

🔐 Authentication & Cryptography

AUTHENTICATION FACTORS + PASSWORD STORAGE
Three factor categories: something you know (password) · have (phone, hardware key) · are (fingerprint, face). Multi-factor combines categories — password alone isn't enough. Passwords are never stored plaintext: hash with a deliberately slow, salted algorithm (bcrypt, scrypt, argon2, PBKDF2). Per-user salt defeats rainbow tables. SHA-256 alone is WRONG for passwords — too fast, no salt.
SYMMETRIC vs ASYMMETRIC
SymmetricAsymmetric (public-key)
KeysSame key both waysPublic encrypts / private decrypts
SpeedFast — the workhorseSlower — wraps a session key
StandardAES-256, AES-GCM (encrypt + integrity)RSA, ECC — basis of TLS, SSH, signing
Cryptographic hashes (SHA-256, BLAKE3) are one-way summaries for checksums & proofs — different from password hashes, which need slowness. Digital signatures: sign a hash with your private key; anyone verifies with your public key → proves authenticity + integrity.
TLS — WHAT PROTECTS MOST TRAFFIC
Handshake: agree on parameters → exchange keys (public key wraps a symmetric session key) → authenticate the server (and optionally client) via certificates. After the handshake, all traffic is symmetrically encrypted. That's the shape of HTTPS, IMAPS, and SSH.
⚠️ FOUR TRAPS
Plaintext passwords — the recurring breach. Fast hashes (MD5/SHA-1/SHA-256) for password storage — you want slowness. Rolling your own crypto — use vetted libraries (libsodium, OpenSSL, BoringSSL). Trusting a certificate without checking the chain or expiration.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Why is SHA-256 the wrong choice for storing passwords?
  1. It's fast and unsalted — password hashing needs slowness + per-user salt
  2. It's not secure enough for any use
  3. It can't produce a fixed-size output
  4. It's asymmetric
Show answer + steps
A. Password hashing wants deliberate slowness (bcrypt/argon2/PBKDF2) + salt; SHA-256 is built for speed, which helps attackers brute-force.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Authentication verifies who you are. Cryptography is the math that makes proofs possible across untrusted networks. Both rely on building blocks — passwords, keys, hashes, certificates — that the OS exposes through APIs. Misuse is how breaches happen.

Core concepts

1. Authentication factors. Something you know (password). Something you have (phone, hardware key). Something you are (fingerprint, face). Multi-factor combines categories. Modern thinking: password alone is not enough; at least two factors for anything sensitive.

2. Password storage — never plain. Always hash, never store plaintext. The hash should be slow on purpose: bcrypt, scrypt, argon2, PBKDF2. Per-user salt prevents rainbow-table attacks. SHA-256 alone is wrong for passwords — too fast, no salt by default. Frameworks provide the right primitives.

3. Symmetric encryption. Same key encrypts and decrypts. AES-256 is the workhorse. Modes (CBC, GCM, CTR) determine guarantees. AES-GCM is the standard recommendation — confidentiality plus authenticated integrity. Key management is harder than the math.

4. Asymmetric (public-key) encryption. Public/private key pairs. Anyone can encrypt with the public key; only the private-key holder can decrypt. RSA, ECC. Slower than symmetric, so usually used to wrap a symmetric session key. Basis of TLS, SSH, signing.

5. Cryptographic hashes. Hash function (SHA-256, BLAKE3) summarizes any input to a fixed-size value. One-way: easy to compute, hard to invert. Used for: passwords (with slow KDF + salt), file checksums, blockchain proofs. Different from password hashes (which need slowness).

6. Digital signatures. Sign by encrypting a hash with your private key; anyone can verify with your public key. Proves authenticity (only you could sign) and integrity (any change invalidates the signature). Basis of code signing, certificates, blockchain transactions.

7. TLS — what protects most network traffic. Three-step handshake: agree on parameters, exchange keys (often using public key to wrap a symmetric session key), authenticate server (and optionally client) via certificates. After handshake, all traffic is symmetrically encrypted. Shape of HTTPS, IMAPS, SSH.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Storing passwords as plain text — the foundational mistake that recurs in breach after breach.
  • Using fast hashes (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256) for password storage — they're built for speed; you want slowness.
  • Building your own crypto — almost always wrong; use vetted libraries (libsodium, OpenSSL, BoringSSL).
  • Trusting any certificate the system presents without checking the chain or expiration.

Quick recap

Authentication uses something you know, have, or are; multi-factor combines them. Passwords must be hashed with slow, salted algorithms. Symmetric encryption (AES-GCM) is fast; asymmetric (RSA, ECC) handles key exchange and signing. TLS protects most network traffic via handshake-then-symmetric. Use vetted libraries; never roll your own.

Glossary

Multi-factor authentication
Authentication using two or more independent factors.
Salt
Per-user random value combined with password before hashing to defeat rainbow tables.
AES-GCM
Symmetric cipher providing both encryption and authentication.
Public-key cryptography
Schemes using paired keys (public for encrypt/verify, private for decrypt/sign).
TLS
Transport Layer Security — protocol securing most modern network traffic.

⚔️ Threats & Defenses

MALWARE CATEGORIES (each needs different response)
TypeBehavior
VirusAttaches to files, spreads on execution
WormSelf-propagates over the network
TrojanLooks legitimate, hides malicious code
RansomwareEncrypts data, demands payment
RootkitHides itself in the kernel
EXPLOIT PRIMITIVES + THEIR DEFENSES
AttackWhat it doesDefense
Buffer overflowWrites past array bounds → overwrites return address/pointerStack canaries, ASLR, DEP/NX, safe languages
Code injectionAttacker data run as code (SQLi, command, XSS)Input validation, parameterized queries, CSP, sandboxing
DDoSOverwhelm a service from many sourcesCapacity, rate limiting, anycast, scrubbing (Cloudflare, AWS Shield)
Privilege escalationGain higher rights than authorizedLeast privilege, sandboxing, KASLR, kPTI
THE NETWORK PERIMETER
Firewalls filter traffic by rules: packet filters (per-packet on IP/port/protocol), stateful (track connection state), application/Layer-7 (inspect payload). IDS detects attack signs (signatures/anomalies) and reports; IPS does the same but actively blocks (Snort, Suricata). Both are part of defense in depth — layered controls, the strategy that actually works.
⚠️ FOUR TRAPS
Perimeter-only defense — once inside, systems are often soft. Disabling ASLR/SELinux/secure boot for convenience causes incidents. Backups reachable from production get encrypted by ransomware too — keep offline/immutable copies. And humans are the most-exploited surface — social engineering beats technical defenses.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Which defense randomizes memory layout to make buffer-overflow exploits harder?
  1. ASLR
  2. DDoS
  3. RBAC
  4. Spooling
Show answer + steps
A. Address Space Layout Randomization randomizes where code/data land, so an attacker can't reliably predict the addresses an overflow needs.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Every OS faces real attackers, and every defense fits somewhere on a spectrum from prevention to detection to recovery. Knowing the canonical threats — buffer overflows, code injection, malware, DDoS — and the defenses against each is the working vocabulary of OS security.

Core concepts

1. Malware categories. Virus: attaches to files, propagates with execution. Worm: self-propagates over network. Trojan: looks legitimate, hides malicious code. Ransomware: encrypts data, demands payment. Rootkit: hides itself in the kernel. Each requires different detection and response.

2. Buffer overflow attacks. Writing past array bounds overwrites adjacent memory — sometimes the return address, sometimes a function pointer. Classic exploit primitive in unsafe languages (C, C++). Defenses: stack canaries, ASLR (random memory layout), DEP/NX (non-executable data pages), bounds checking in safe languages.

3. Code injection. Get attacker-controlled data interpreted as code. SQL injection (most famous). Command injection. Cross-site scripting (XSS). Buffer overflows can lead to code execution. Defense: input validation, parameterized queries, content security policies, sandboxing.

4. DDoS — Distributed Denial of Service. Overwhelm a service with traffic from many sources. Volume-based, protocol-based, application-layer. Defenses: capacity, rate limiting, anycast distribution, scrubbing services (Cloudflare, AWS Shield). Hard to fully eliminate; reduce impact by overprovisioning and filtering.

5. Privilege escalation. Attacker gains higher privileges than authorized — local user becomes root, web server breaks out of sandbox. Often combines a small bug with access to a privileged target (setuid binary, kernel syscall). Defenses: least privilege, sandboxing, kernel hardening (KASLR, kPTI).

6. Firewalls. Filter network traffic by rules. Packet filters: per-packet decisions on source/dest IP, port, protocol. Stateful firewalls: track connection state. Application firewalls: inspect payload. Layer-7 firewalls in modern infrastructure. First line of network defense.

7. Intrusion detection systems (IDS) and prevention (IPS). IDS: monitors for signs of attack (signatures, anomalies). Reports. IPS: same but actively blocks. Snort, Suricata. Network-based or host-based. Part of defense in depth; sees what gets past the firewall.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Treating perimeter defense as enough — once an attacker is inside, the inside is often soft.
  • Disabling protective measures (ASLR, SELinux, secure boot) for convenience — common cause of incidents.
  • Backups that are accessible from production — ransomware encrypts those too. Offline / immutable backups matter.
  • Focusing only on technical defenses while users can be socially engineered — humans are the most exploited surface.

Quick recap

Malware: viruses, worms, Trojans, ransomware, rootkits. Buffer overflows and code injection are classic exploit primitives. DDoS overwhelms with traffic; rate limiting and scrubbing help. Privilege escalation combines small bugs with privileged targets. Firewalls filter network traffic; IDS/IPS detect intrusions. Defense in depth — layered controls — is the strategy that works.

Glossary

Malware
Malicious software including viruses, worms, Trojans, ransomware, rootkits.
Buffer overflow
Writing past array bounds; classic exploit primitive in unsafe languages.
DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service)
Attack overwhelming a service with traffic from many sources.
Firewall
Network device or software filtering traffic based on rules.
IDS / IPS
Intrusion Detection / Prevention System — monitors and optionally blocks attacks.
📊 FIGURE — the vocabulary this section is tested on
🎯 EXAM TIP
The CIA triad is Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability — the three core security goals, and a near-certain exam item. Note that phishing attacks the person, not the software, which is why patching cannot stop it; patches close known vulnerabilities in the code, and only work if they are actually applied.

📖 Worked example — a hard scheduling problem, start to finish

WORKED EXAMPLE — average waiting time under two schedulers
Three jobs arrive at t=0 with bursts: P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3.

FCFS (arrival order): P1 waits 0, P2 waits 24, P3 waits 27 → average = (0+24+27)/3 = 17.
SJF (shortest first: P2, P3, P1): P2 waits 0, P3 waits 3, P1 waits 6 → average = (0+3+6)/3 = 3.

Same jobs, 5-6× better waiting time — the “convoy effect” of one long job blocking short ones is exactly what SJF eliminates. Method: line the jobs on a timeline, read each job’s start time = its waiting time, average them.
⚠️ PREEMPTIVE CHANGES THE TIMELINE
Round-robin and SRTF can INTERRUPT the running job — recompute the timeline at every quantum/arrival. FCFS and plain SJF never interrupt. Check which variant the question names before drawing the timeline.

Turning schedules into numbers

Every CPU-scheduling problem reduces to building a Gantt chart, then reading two metrics off it. Turnaround time (TAT) = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time (WT) = TAT − burst = time spent in the ready queue. Average either metric by summing across all processes and dividing by n.

The algorithms differ only in which ready process you dispatch next. FCFS dispatches by arrival order (non-preemptive, prone to the convoy effect). SJF (non-preemptive) picks the smallest total burst among processes that have already arrived. SRTF is preemptive SJF: at every arrival you compare the new job's burst against the running job's remaining time and switch if smaller. Round-Robin gives each process one time quantum, then requeues it at the tail; a newly arrived job typically joins the tail before the preempted job. Priority dispatches the highest priority (usually lowest number); starvation is fixed with aging.

Synchronization and deadlock

A race condition occurs when the result depends on interleaving of unsynchronized accesses to shared data. A correct critical-section solution must satisfy mutual exclusion, progress (only contenders decide, and selection cannot be postponed indefinitely), and bounded waiting. A mutex is a locking primitive with ownership (only the locker unlocks); a counting semaphore tracks N units and has no owner. In the bounded-buffer producer-consumer problem you need three: empty, full, and a binary mutex.

Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. Prevention breaks one structurally; avoidance (Banker's algorithm) uses advance claims to stay in a safe state; detection allows deadlock, then recovers.

📖 Worked example — a hard memory problem, start to finish

WORKED EXAMPLE — page faults under LRU
Reference string 1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 2 with 3 frames, LRU replacement:

1 → fault [1]  ·  2 → fault [1,2]  ·  3 → fault [1,2,3]  ·  1 → HIT (1 becomes most-recent)  ·  4 → fault, evict least-recently-used = 2 → [3,1,4]  ·  2 → fault, evict 3 → [1,4,2].

Total: 5 faults, 1 hit. Bookkeeping is everything: after every reference (hit OR fault), reorder by recency. Most wrong answers come from forgetting that a HIT also refreshes recency.
⚠️ LRU ≠ FIFO
FIFO evicts the OLDEST-LOADED page (arrival time, never refreshed); LRU evicts the least-recently-USED (refreshed on every touch). The same reference string usually gives different fault counts — and the exam asks both on purpose.

Address translation and replacement

With page size 2^k, the low k bits of a logical address are the offset and the high bits are the page number. Translate by looking the page number up in the page table to get a frame number, then physical address = frame × page_size + offset. A TLB caches recent translations; effective access time weights the hit path (TLB + memory) and miss path (TLB + page-table memory access + data memory access) by the hit ratio.

For a reference string and a fixed frame count, count faults by simulation. FIFO evicts the oldest-loaded page; it can suffer Belady's anomaly (more frames yielding more faults). LRU evicts the least-recently-used page and is a stack algorithm (anomaly-free). Optimal (OPT) evicts the page used farthest in the future — the theoretical minimum, not implementable. When a process lacks enough frames to hold its working set (the set of pages referenced in the recent Δ window), it thrashes: page-fault rate explodes and CPU utilization collapses.

Files and disks

Contiguous allocation is fast but fragments; linked allocation kills random access; indexed allocation (the Unix inode with direct plus single/double/triple indirect blocks) balances both. Maximum file size = (direct + pointers-per-indirect-block × levels) × block size, where pointers-per-block = block_size / pointer_size.

Disk scheduling minimizes total head movement. FCFS serves in request order; SSTF serves the nearest request (risking starvation); SCAN (elevator) sweeps to one end and reverses; C-SCAN sweeps one direction then jumps back to the start for uniform wait. Sum the absolute cylinder differences along the service order to get total seek distance.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

📋 Introduction to Operating Systems

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Role of the OS

▸ THE TWO JOBS ① Resource manager — CPU, memory, disk, and network are finite; the OS allocates, protects, and shares them among all programs (it's the arbiter). ② Abstraction layer — hardware is messy (sectors, interrupts, frames); the OS exposes clean interfaces: files, processes, sockets, virtual…

⚠ TWO NAMING TRAPS "The OS" has a narrow meaning (just the kernel) and a broad one (kernel + libraries + shell + utilities) — clarify which. And the two purposes of an OS are in TENSION: user convenience vs efficient…

OS Services & System Calls

▸ WHAT A SYSTEM CALL IS A controlled user→kernel transition: user code sets up arguments, executes a special instruction ( syscall on x86-64, svc on ARM), the CPU jumps to a kernel handler, the kernel VALIDATES and does the work, and the result returns in a register. Slower than a function call — and…

⚠ LIBRARY ≠ SYSCALL printf is a LIBRARY function; write is the SYSCALL underneath. And always check return values — failed syscalls silently corrupt state.

OS Structure & Bootstrapping

⚠ THE CONTAINER TRAP Containers ≠ VMs: each VM has its OWN kernel; containers all share the host's. And microkernel ≠ always slow — modern message-passing narrows the gap.

"},"C191/cheat/c2":{"body":"

📋 Processes & Threads

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Process Concept & PCB

▸ PROGRAM vs PROCESS A program is a passive file on disk. A process is the ACTIVE execution of it — and many processes can run the same program at once, each with its own state. The kernel's record of a process is the PCB (Process Control Block): PID, program counter, registers, memory map, open…

⚠ ISOLATION IS THE POINT Each process has its own PRIVATE address space — a bug in one can't scribble on another. Threads share memory; processes don't. And a forked child is logically separate (copy-on-write…

Process Creation, Termination

⚠ THE CLASSIC BUGS Forgetting wait() breeds zombies until the system can't fork. And fork COPIES while exec REPLACES — mixing them up is the #1 exam trap.

Threads & Multithreading Models

▸ THREAD vs PROCESS — the sharing table Each thread OWNS: program counter, registers, its stack. Threads in one process SHARE: heap, code, open files. Creating a thread is far cheaper than forking — but a crash in one thread typically kills the WHOLE process. Why multithread: parallelism (cores),…

⚠ THREE TRAPS Thread-per-request caps servers at thousands (stack memory) — pool or go M:N. Shared mutable state without synchronization = race conditions (next chapter). And concurrency ≠ parallelism : a single-core…

Inter-Process Communication (IPC)

⚠ THE CLASSIC MISTAKES Shared memory without synchronization = data races. Signals can't carry data — don't try. And Unix sockets beat TCP loopback 2–3× for local-only traffic.

"},"C191/cheat/c3":{"body":"

📋 CPU Scheduling & Synchronization

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

CPU Scheduling Algorithms

▸ THE GOALS CONFLICT Throughput · latency/response time · fairness · predictability · energy — no algorithm wins them all; production schedulers balance.

⚠ EXAM MATH Wait excludes CPU time; turnaround includes it. Average wait is THE standard comparison metric — expect to compute it.

Synchronization & Critical Sections

▸ THE DEFINITION A race condition : two+ threads access shared state, at least one WRITES, with no synchronization — the outcome depends on interleaving order. The hardest bugs to reproduce; production load makes them frequent.

⚠ THE FOUR PITFALLS Believing one-liners are atomic · C's volatile is NOT synchronization · locking each operation but not the multi-step invariant · "works on my machine" shipping — production will find the race.

Semaphores, Mutexes, Monitors

⚠ THE FOUR CLASSIC BUGS ① Forgetting to release on the ERROR path — use try/finally, RAII, or with. ② Signaling a condition variable without holding its lock. ③ ALWAYS wait in a while loop re-checking the predicate —…

Classic Problems & Deadlock

▸ THE FOUR COFFMAN CONDITIONS — ALL required for deadlock ① Mutual exclusion · ② Hold and wait · ③ No preemption · ④ Circular wait . Remove ANY one and deadlock is impossible. The most practical prevention: kill circular wait with a global lock ordering .

⚠ THE SUBTLE ONE Holding a lock while calling UNKNOWN code (callbacks, listeners) — it may acquire other locks and complete a cycle you can't see.

"},"C191/cheat/c4":{"body":"

📋 Memory Management

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Contiguous Memory Allocation

▸ THE PRE-PAGING PROBLEM Multiple programs must coexist in physical RAM, each in a contiguous region. Hardware protection: base + limit registers — physical = virtual + base; trap if virtual ≥ limit. Simple, fast, hardware-enforced.

⚠ THE TRAPS Best-fit "sounds smart" but first-fit usually wins in practice. Compaction is NOT practical at scale — paging (next lesson) sidesteps the whole problem by making contiguity virtual.

Paging & Page Tables

▸ THE BIG IDEA Split virtual memory into fixed-size pages (typically 4 KB) and physical memory into same-size frames . The per-process page table maps page → frame; the MMU translates every access. Any page can live in any frame (or on disk) — contiguity becomes an illusion, and each process gets a…

⚠ TWO EXAM NOTES Don't confuse the virtual layout (process view) with physical (kernel view). And page size isn't always 4 KB — huge pages (2 MB, 1 GB) exist for large-memory apps.

Segmentation

▸ THE IDEA Treat memory as VARIABLE-sized logical segments matching program structure — code (read-only, executable), data, stack, heap. Addresses are (segment, offset) ; the per-process segment table holds each segment's base + limit: if offset ≥ limit → fault, else physical = base + offset.

⚠ TWO MODERN-USAGE TRAPS Today "segment" usually means a region of an executable FILE — different from old memory segmentation. And modern Linux/macOS/Windows use PAGING as the primary mechanism; segmentation survives…

Virtual Memory & Demand Paging

▸ DEMAND PAGING Pages load only on FIRST access: the entry is marked not-present, access triggers a page fault , the kernel allocates a frame, loads from disk, resumes the instruction. When no free frame exists, a victim must be EVICTED — that choice is page replacement.

⚠ TWO DISTINCTIONS Pure LRU (timestamp every access) is too expensive — the clock approximation is the real implementation. And replacement policy (WHO gets evicted) ≠ allocation policy (HOW MANY frames each process…

Thrashing and Working Set

▸ THE FAILURE MODE Thrashing: collective memory needs exceed physical RAM → every process faults, evicting each other's pages endlessly. Signature: CPU utilization PLUMMETS while disk I/O SPIKES — the system pages instead of working. Counter-intuitively worst when running the MOST processes.

⚠ FOR PROGRAMMERS Memory pressure shows up as terrible LATENCY long before anything is killed. Watch page-fault rate, swap activity, and resident set size — a box with a calm CPU graph can be unusably slow from paging. The fix is less memory demand or more RAM — not a faster CPU.

"},"C191/cheat/c5":{"body":"

📋 Storage & File Systems

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

File System Interface

▸ WHAT A FILE IS (OS-SIDE) A named, persistent collection of bytes + metadata the OS keeps for it: size, type, owner, permissions, timestamps, location. Your program sees bytes; the OS does the bookkeeping. Every operation (create/open/read/write/seek/close/delete/rename/truncate) maps to a system…

⚠ FOUR TRAPS Hard link (another name for the SAME inode) ≠ symlink (a path pointing to a path). Unix ctime is metadata-change time, NOT creation. Build paths with OS-aware utilities, not string concatenation. And…

File System Implementation

▸ THE THREE LAYERS Top: FS API (open/read/write) · Middle: FS implementation (inodes, blocks, allocation) · Bottom: block device driver . Each layer abstracts the one below — debugging often means reasoning downward through them.

⚠ FOUR TRAPS Millions of tiny files can exhaust inodes despite free space. write() lands in the page cache, not disk — fsync forces the flush. Never compare FS performance without naming the workload. Don't pick FAT…

Disk Scheduling Algorithms

▸ THE HDD SEEK PROBLEM Moving the head between tracks (a seek ) costs milliseconds — the slow part. Sequential reads (no head movement) are ~ 100× faster than random. So the order of requests determines total seek time, and that's what these algorithms optimize.

⚠ FOUR TRAPS SCAN/C-SCAN on an SSD wastes effort on a non-problem. SSTF without aging starves far-out requests. Interactive (latency) vs bulk (throughput) requests want different policies. And real time = seek +…

I/O Systems

⚠ FOUR TRAPS Polling a slow device wastes CPU when interrupts would yield — yet at very high IOPS (NVMe), polling can beat interrupt overhead. Skipping DMA means byte-copying can exceed wire bandwidth. And synchronous I/O in a hot path stalls the caller — buffer or go asynchronous when the device is slower than the producer.

"},"C191/cheat/c6":{"body":"

📋 Protection & Security

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Protection Mechanisms

▸ THE PROTECTION QUESTION Who (subject) can do what (operation) to which object? Subject = user/process · Operation = read/write/execute/delete · Object = file/socket/process/device. Every access-control model answers this triple. The guiding rule: least privilege — each component gets only the…

⚠ FOUR TRAPS Running services as root "because easier" — compromise = total access. Unix permissions alone aren't enough for shared-user systems (need ACLs/RBAC). Leaving SELinux in permissive mode "to make it work"…

Authentication & Cryptography

⚠ FOUR TRAPS Plaintext passwords — the recurring breach. Fast hashes (MD5/SHA-1/SHA-256) for password storage — you want slowness. Rolling your own crypto — use vetted libraries (libsodium, OpenSSL, BoringSSL).…

Common Threats & Defenses

⚠ FOUR TRAPS Perimeter-only defense — once inside, systems are often soft. Disabling ASLR/SELinux/secure boot for convenience causes incidents. Backups reachable from production get encrypted by ransomware too — keep at least one copy offline or immutable (the 3-2-1 backup rule exists for exactly this reason).

Using round-robin scheduling with a 4 ms quantum, what is the average waiting time?","options":["2.5 ms","4.0 ms","3.5 ms","7.5 ms"],"correct":2,"explain":"P1 runs 0-4, P2 runs 4-7 (done), P1 runs 7-8 (done); waiting is 3 ms for P1 and 4 ms for P2, averaging 3.5 ms."},{"id":"fresh_C191_16","topic":"Priority scheduling","text":"A low-priority process never runs because higher-priority processes keep arriving.
